cues.text: A Monk's Unspoken Doubt

Sometime in the eighth century, in the small hill city of Lanciano in what is now Italy's Abruzzo region, an unnamed monk of the Basilian order was preparing to offer Holy Mass at the church of Saints Longinus and Domitian.
Catholic tradition holds that this monk was bound by vows and daily entrusted with the sacred mysteries.
Yet he had begun to be troubled inwardly by doubts about the Real Presence of Christ in the consecrated bread and wine—the very teaching he professed every time he stood at the altar.
The Words of Consecration
According to the tradition preserved at Lanciano, the moment came as the monk pronounced the words of consecration over the host and chalice.

Where a moment before there had been bread and wine, he now saw before him what appeared to be living flesh and blood — the blood, tradition says, coagulating almost immediately into five separate globules of differing size and shape.
Tradition records the monk’s words to the startled congregation gathered around the altar: “Behold the Flesh and Blood of our most beloved Christ.”
Whatever precise words passed his lips that day, the account handed down insists the moment was not private.
Others in the church were said to have seen the same transformation.
Word of it spread quickly through the surrounding countryside—a doubting priest's private struggle becoming, in an instant, a public sign for anyone who would come to see it.
Flesh That Would Not Decay
What sets Lanciano apart from a purely private vision or a fading local legend is its physical persistence.
The flesh and blood were kept at the church, then entrusted to the Conventual Franciscan friars, who assumed custody of the shrine in 1252.
In 1713, they were placed in an ornate silver and rock-crystal reliquary crafted by Neapolitan artisans.
In essentials, it is the same vessel that still holds them today in the Church of San Francesco, built over the site of the original small church.

Across the centuries the relics were opened for inspection at several points, and each time, witnesses reported, the flesh and blood appeared unchanged: neither decayed, powdered, nor visibly altered by time.

For a relic exposed to open air rather than sealed and treated by any preservative process, that alone struck generations of observers as remarkable, well before anyone thought to examine it with a microscope.
Centuries of Testing
The most rigorous scrutiny came in November 1970, when Archbishop Pacifico Perantoni of Lanciano, acting with authorization from Rome, asked Dr. Odoardo Linoli to examine the relics.
Linoli was professor of anatomy, histology, and clinical microscopy, and head of pathological anatomy at the hospital of Arezzo.
Assisted by Professor Ruggero Bertelli of the University of Siena, Linoli extracted small samples with great care and studied them for several months before presenting his findings on March 4, 1971.
Published that same year in the Italian medical journal Quaderni Sclavo di Diagnostica Clinica e di Laboratori , Linoli's report was studied again a decade later, in 1981.
The second examination used a separate, previously untouched fragment and confirmed what the first had found.
This was not devotional testimony alone; it was a peer-reviewed clinical study, open to scrutiny by the wider scientific community.
What the Science Found

Linoli's analysis concluded that the flesh was genuine human tissue — specifically myocardial tissue, the muscle of the heart, including fibers of the endocardium consistent with the wall of a hollow organ.
The blood, he found, was authentic human blood of type AB, containing mineral and protein proportions consistent with fresh blood rather than a long-decayed sample.
What Linoli could not offer was any natural account of how such tissue had survived exposed to open air for well over a millennium without decomposing.

Some later, more sweeping claims about international scientific commissions endorsing his findings have not held up to scrutiny and should be set aside; what remains solid is Linoli's own published, peer-reviewed 1971 study and its 1981 confirmation.
Catholic scientists today rightly caution that laboratory findings, however striking, can describe what the relic is made of without constituting theological proof.
The miracle's meaning belongs, finally, to faith, even where the tissue itself resists a purely natural explanation.
Legacy
Today the relics of Lanciano rest above the altar of the Church of San Francesco, visible to any pilgrim who climbs the steps of that Abruzzese hill town, much as they have been for twelve centuries.
Among the countless visitors have been ordinary believers and doubters alike, drawn by a relic that asks nothing of them but to look.
Among them, tradition holds, was a young priest from Poland who came quietly to Lanciano, years before the world knew him as John Paul II.
We find in Lanciano something more than an object of historical curiosity: a monk's unguarded doubt met not with condemnation.
Instead, it received a sign meant to console every heart that has ever struggled to believe what it could not fully see.
For every Catholic who kneels at Mass and hears the same words of consecration spoken again, Lanciano stands as a quiet, enduring witness.
It testifies that Christ meant precisely what he said at the Last Supper — that this is, truly, his Body and his Blood.
